content.content:
# Mend

**An agent that reads its own [neatlogs](https://neatlogs.com) traces, fixes its own code, and
keeps the fix only if a full re-run gets better.** Built during
[neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon), 10–12 October 2026, by team The Good Engineers.

**Website:** https://thegoodengineers.github.io/mend/ · **Full data report:**
[report.html](https://thegoodengineers.github.io/mend/report.html) · **Build log:**
[hackathon.md](hackathon.md)

**Demo video (2:43):** [`video/demo/mend-demo.mp4`](video/demo/mend-demo.mp4) · **Keep/revert rules:** [`docs/GATE.md`](docs/GATE.md) · **Evidence index:** [`evidence/INDEX.md`](evidence/INDEX.md)

[![Mend website](docs/img/site-hero.png)](https://thegoodengineers.github.io/mend/)

[![Live recording: original worker fails, repaired worker passes](docs/img/live-result.png)](video/live/mend-live.mp4)
*Live recording (1:55, click): same task, same model. Original worker failed in 15 turns; after
self-repair it passed in 4.*

Every number in this README comes from a file in [`runs/`](runs/) or [`evidence/`](evidence/).
If a number has no file behind it, it is not here.

## For judges: 60 seconds

| neatHack evidence item | Where to check it |
|---|---|
| The agent improved (before/after with numbers) | [rounds table](#self-repair-rounds-five-kept-three-reverted), [3-vs-3 repeat runs](#repeatable-not-lucky-same-28-tasks-3-runs-each), [held-out test](#held-out-test-10-bugs-the-supervisor-never-saw), [real-world library](#real-world-test-bugs-in-an-open-source-library-it-never-saw); [live recording](video/live/mend-live.mp4) |
| You used neatlogs | [traced call](evidence/t02-first-traced-call.txt), [trace read back over MCP](evidence/t04-trace-readback.txt), [task 23 before](evidence/task23-before-trace.json) / [after](evidence/task23-after-trace.json) traces; 4 regression-guard detections ([`mend/detections.py`](mend/detections.py)); every gate verdict is also written back into neatlogs as a `mend-gate` trace, one span per keep rule, and a detection flags each revert ([`mend/audit.py`](mend/audit.py), [read-back](evidence/gate-audit-readback.md)); second opinion from neatlogs' own [neatroots](evidence/neatroots-che
| You used Entire | [round 4 checkpoint](https://entire.io/gh/thegoodengineers/mend/commit/7e2148e201fdaa9b2b3f921d1f2651950f537205) (the supervisor's own Claude Code session); the supervisor reads past checkpoints back as repair memory; [who wrote the worker](https://thegoodengineers.github.io/mend/#provenance): `entire blame` shows 69% of the worker's prompt was written by Mend's own sessions |
| You used cfo.ai | [business plan](docs/business-plan.md) and its [cfo.ai export](docs/business-plan-cfo-ai.xlsx) |
| The improvement is real, not noise | [paired statistics per decision](#self-repair-rounds-five-kept-three-reverted) (rounds 3–5 solid; rounds 1–2 rest on one task flip, said plainly); [leave-one-out ablation](evidence/ablation.json) (removing round 5: +61% tokens); 2 fixes reverted by the gate; re-check every decision [in your browser](https://thegoodengineers.github.io/mend/#verify) |
| It knows when not to fix itself | [ask once, remember](#is-self-healing-self-defeating): a fix that is a choice stops for a person, and the answer becomes a precedent (answers neatlogs' "Self-healing is self-defeating") |
| The agent recovers from failures | [run_tests timed out, then fixed](evidence/t17-recovery-from-timeout.txt); in the live recording a tool call fails ("Permission denied") and the worker carries on |
| You built in public | [first #neatHack post](https://x.com/theintrodev/status/2108851736765141188) |
| Code written during the hackathon | [commit history](https://github.com/thegoodengineers/mend/commits/main) (first commit: plans only, as the rules allow) |

Every number in this README is recomputed from the run files by [`mend/verify.py`](mend/verify.py) on
every push ([CI](https://github.com/thegoodengineers/mend/actions)).

## How it works

```
worker agent ──runs 29 tasks──▶ neatlogs traces every model call and tool call
      ▲                                   │
      │                                   ▼  (neatlogs MCP: get_trace_context)
 keep or revert ◀── re-run the suite ◀── supervisor diagnoses failed + wasteful runs
                                          │
                                          ▼
                     Claude Code applies ONE general fix to the worker,
                     committed and captured as an Entire checkpoint
```

1. **Run.** A worker agent ([`mend/worker.py`](mend/worker.py), Claude Haiku 4.5) fixes planted
   bugs in a small invoicing library ([`sandbox/`](sandbox/), 37 tests). There are 29 tasks in
   [`tasks/tasks.json`](tasks/tasks.json). Pass means the library's test suite passes, judged
   by the runner, not by the agent.
2. **Trace.** Every model call and tool call is a span in neatlogs (one WORKFLOW span per task,
   TOOL spans per tool call). Each run file stores the task's neatlogs trace ID.
3. **Diagnose.** The supervisor ([`mend/supervisor.py`](mend/supervisor.py), Claude Opus 5.5)
   pulls the traces of failed tasks and the slowest passing tasks back over the neatlogs MCP
   server ([`mend/traces.py`](mend/traces.py)). It writes a diagnosis naming the failing step
   and one general fix.
4. **Patch.** Headless Claude Code applies the fix to `mend/worker.py` or
   `mend/prompts/worker.md` only. A guard rejects patches that touch other files or name
   specific library code.
5. **Prove.** The suite re-runs. The patch is kept if more tasks pass, or the same tasks pass
   with at least 15% fewer tokens. Otherwise it is reverted with `git revert`.

### Is self-healing self-defeating?

neatlogs' founder argues that a loop which fixes every mistake drifts toward the median, unless
someone defines what "better" means
([Self-healing is self-defeating](https://neatlogs.com/blog/self-healing-is-self-defeating)).
His prescription has three steps: automate everything that isn't a choice, ask someone when it
is, and remember the answer. Here is where Mend stands on each:

- **Automate what isn't a choice.** Mend only repairs things with an objective answer. The
  library's own test suite judges each task, the runner does the judging (not the agent), and
  token cost is counted by the API. Mend never repairs taste, tone or policy.
- **"Better" is defined by people.** The keep rule is code we wrote (`one_round()` in
  [`mend/supervisor.py`](mend/supervisor.py)), written out in [`docs/GATE.md`](docs/GATE.md).
  The supervisor may not change it, because only two files may change. Rounds 6, 7 and 8 show
  the gate saying no.
- **Remember the answer.** Every round, whether kept, reverted or rejected, is a record in
  `runs/`, and the Claude Code session behind each fix is an Entire checkpoint. Both are fed back
  into the next diagnosis, so a failed fix is not proposed again.
- **Ask someone when it is a choice** (added 11 Oct, `6a3b2c2`). Every diagnosis now states whether its
  fix is a *correction* or a *choice*. A choice trades one valid behaviour for another that no test
  or token count decides. A choice stops the round before any patch and writes the question to
  `runs/<id>.question.json`. A person answers with `python -m mend.supervisor --answer <id> "..."`.
  The answer goes to [`docs/precedents.json`](docs/precedents.json), and every later diagnosis must
  follow it, so each question is asked once. Round 7 was the first round with this step: it judged
  its fix a correction, and the gate then reverted it. No real choice has come up yet, so the
  ask path is shown only by a unit test.

### What makes this more than a loop

Several self-repair loops were built for neatHack. Here is what Mend shows beyond "it got better
once":
- **8 rounds**, 5 kept and **3 reverted** by the gate, with every decision re-checkable in the
  browser ([site, "Check it yourself"](https://thegoodengineers.github.io/mend/#verify)) or with
  `python -m mend.verify`.
- **Held-out bugs** the supervisor never saw: 9/10 → 10/10.
- **A real open-source library** it never saw (inflection): 2–3/8 → 8/8.
- **Repeat runs:** 3 runs before and 3 after, on the same 28 tasks.
- **Repair memory** read back from Entire checkpoints.
- **A second opinion** from neatlogs' own neatroots checker.

## Results

### Self-repair rounds (five kept, three reverted)

| # | What Mend changed in itself | Solved | Tokens | Commit | Diagnosis |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Added an exact-replace `edit_file` tool; steered edits away from whole-file rewrites | 27 → 28 / 28 | 933,181 → 851,463 (−8.8%) | `e8a6baf` | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T09-15-17.diagnosis.md) |
| 2 | `edit_file` shows the current text of a near match on a miss; clearer line prefixes | 28 → 29 / 29 | 1,005,203 → 894,839 (−11.0%) | `f9dae91` | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T10-17-27.diagnosis.md) |
| 3 | Test-first workflow; stop as soon as the suite passes | 29 → 29 / 29 | 894,839 → 618,906 (−30.8%) | `931ea51` | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T10-30-26-after.diagnosis.md) |
| 4 | Loop hands the worker the file list up front and finishes automatically once the full suite passes after an edit | 29 → 29 / 29 | 618,906 → 432,858 (−30.1%) | [`7e2148e`](https://entire.io/gh/thegoodengineers/mend/commit/7e2148e201fdaa9b2b3f921d1f2651950f537205) (Entire checkpoint) | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T10-41-18-after.diagnosis.md) |
| 5 | Loop re-runs the full suite automatically after any successful edit and finishes on green | 29 → 29 / 29 | 456,563 → 347,960 (−23.8%) | [`c07f702`](https://entire.io/gh/thegoodengineers/mend/commit/c07f70237b8f640e5435edbec09dbb6976c49ed8) (Entire checkpoint) | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T11-18-45.diagnosis.md) |
| 6 | `edit_file` takes a list of edits so a whole fix lands in one call | 29 → 29 / 29 | 347,960 → 361,174 (+3.8%) | `49c99e2`, **reverted** by `b5e788d` | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T11-50-52-after.diagnosis.md) |
| 7 | `read_file` returns the whole file by default instead of a 200-line page | 29 → 29 / 29 | 302,153 → 288,229 (−4.6%) | `723015f`, **reverted** by `d1aabc9` | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T13-28-51.diagnosis.md) |
| 8 | Prompt: don't read tests; map the failing test to its source module; trust the traceback over the report | 29 → 29 / 29 | 302,153 → 368,440 (+21.9%) | `badd7dd`, **reverted** by `a403b68` | [diagnosis](runs/2026-10-10T13-28-51-d2.diagnosis.md) |

Round records: the `*.round.json` files in [`runs/`](runs/). Rounds 2 and 3 were run back to back with
`python -m mend.supervisor <run> --rounds 2`; rounds 4-8 ran from a clean runner clone. **Round 8** was the first under [gate amendment 1](docs/GATE.md); it made the worker significantly worse (+21.9% tokens, paired interval [1.099, 1.355] entirely above 1) and was reverted. **Round 7** (11 Oct, the first run with the ask-once judgment step, which judged its fix a correction, not a choice) was also reverted: −4.6% tokens is under the 15% bar. **Round 6 was reverted automatically:** it still solved 29/29 but used 3.8% more tokens, so the gate rejected it. Round 5 also created its own neatlogs

**How sure is each decision?** The gate looks at one re-run. Each task runs both before and
after, so the comparison can be paired per task ([`mend/stats.py`](mend/stats.py), following
Miller, [*Adding Error Bars to Evals*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640); output in
[`evidence/gate-stats.json`](evidence/gate-stats.json)):

| Round | Tasks fixed / broken | Sign test p | Tokens after ÷ before | 95% interval (tasks resampled) | Gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 / 0 | 1.0 | 0.912 | [0.73, 1.156] | kept |
| 2 | 1 / 0 | 1.0 | 0.89 | [0.749, 1.042] | kept |
| 3 | 0 / 0 | 1.0 | 0.692 | [0.609, 0.788] | kept |
| 4 | 0 / 0 | 1.0 | 0.699 | [0.642, 0.764] | kept |
| 5 | 0 / 0 | 1.0 | 0.762 | [0.702, 0.824] | kept |
| 6 | 0 / 0 | 1.0 | 1.038 | [0.91, 1.194] | reverted |
| 7 | 0 / 0 | 1.0 | 0.954 | [0.82, 1.113] | reverted |
| 8 | 0 / 0 | 1.0 | 1.219 | [1.099, 1.355] | reverted (amended gate) |

What this says, plainly:
- **Rounds 3–5 are solid.** Each token cut's whole 95% interval sits below 0.85, the gate's own
  threshold.
- **Rounds 1 and 2 were kept on a single task flipping** from fail to pass. That alone is not
  statistically convincing (p = 1.0), and their token intervals include "no change". Round 1 is
  backed separately by the 3-vs-3 repeat runs below, where every repaired run solved more tasks than
  every original run (28, 28, 28 vs 27, 26, 27), and task 23 passed 3 of 3 times instead of 0 of 3.
- **Round 6's revert was right.** Its interval spans 1, so nothing was gained. Round 7 (−4.6%) is the
  same: its interval [0.82, 1.113] also spans 1.
- **Round 8 made things worse.** Its whole interval [1.099, 1.355] is above 1, so the revert was
  clearly right.

**Caveat:** the interval resamples tasks, not repeated runs, so it does not capture one task's
run-to-run noise.

**Which fixes actually carry the gain? (leave-one-out ablation)** We took today's worker, removed
one kept fix with `git revert`, and re-ran all 29 tasks once
([`scripts/ablation.py`](scripts/ablation.py) → [`evidence/ablation.json`](evidence/ablation.json),
run files in [`runs/ablation/`](runs/ablation/)). Today's worker, run 3 times: 29/29 each time,
302,153–347,960 tokens.

| Fix removed | Solved | Tokens | vs today's mean |
|---|---|---|---|
| Round 5: auto re-run the suite after an edit, finish on green | 29/29 | 535,826 | +61% |
| Round 3: test-first workflow, stop on green | 29/29 | 461,763 | +39% |
| Round 2: `edit_file` shows the near match on a miss | 29/29 | 353,131 | +6% |

What this says:
- **Rounds 5 and 3 carry the savings.** Removing either one costs far more than run-to-run noise.
- **Round 2 adds little on its own today.** Its run lands just above today's range, which matches
  the paired statistics above, where round 2 rested on one task flip.
- **Rounds 1 and 4 cannot be removed alone.** Their reverts conflict, because later fixes build on
  them; for example, every later round uses round 1's `edit_file`.
- **No single removable fix changes the solve rate.** It stays 29/29 each time; the remaining
  fixes compensate.

Each ablation is one run.

**The first bug Mend found in itself.** The worker read only the first 200 lines of the
233-line `ledger.py`, then rewrote the whole file to change one word. That silently deleted
everything after line 200. Task 23 failed at the 15-turn limit; after the fix it passed in 8
turns.

### What changed in the worker's behaviour

These counts were read back from the neatlogs traces of every task in each run
([`scripts/tool_usage.py`](scripts/tool_usage.py) → [`evidence/tool-usage.json`](evidence/tool-usage.json),
0 traces missing):

| Run | Worker | Whole-file writes | `edit_file` calls | Test runs | Model calls |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [09-15-17](runs/2026-10-10T09-15-17.json) (28 tasks) | original | 31 | — | 75 | 235 |
| [09-31-07](runs/2026-10-10T09-31-07-after.json) (28 tasks) | after round 1 | 2 | 36 | 72 | 242 |
| [10-41-18](runs/2026-10-10T10-41-18-after.json) (29 tasks) | after round 3 | 0 | 32 | 56 | 174 |
| [11-50-52](runs/2026-10-10T11-50-52-after.json) (29 tasks) | after round 5 | 0 | 33 | 59 | 107 |

Round 1 replaced the destructive habit, rewriting whole files, with precise edits. Rounds 3–5
cut wasted turns, so model calls fell by more than half.

"""How sure is each gate decision? Paired statistics over the same tasks, before vs after a fix.

    python -m mend.stats     # -> evidence/gate-stats.json, one entry per round

The gate looks at one re-run. Because every task runs both before and after, the comparison can be
paired per task, which removes most run-to-run noise (Miller 2024, "Adding Error Bars to Evals",
arXiv:2411.00640):
- passes: exact two-sided sign test (McNemar) on the tasks that flipped between pass and fail;
- tokens: 95% paired bootstrap interval for total-after / total-before, resampling tasks.
"""

import json
import random
from math import comb

from mend.tasks import ROOT

RUNS = ROOT / "runs"
OUT = ROOT / "evidence" / "gate-stats.json"
BOOT = 10_000


def sign_test(fixed: int, broke: int) -> float:
    """Exact two-sided p-value that fixes and breaks are equally likely (McNemar's exact test)."""
    n = fixed + broke
    if n == 0:
        return 1.0
    k = min(fixed, broke)
    return min(1.0, 2 * sum(comb(n, i) for i in range(k + 1)) / 2 ** n)


def token_ratio_ci(pairs: list[tuple[int, int]], seed: int = 0) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Total-after / total-before, with a 95% bootstrap interval over tasks."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ratio = sum(a for _, a in pairs) / sum(b for b, _ in pairs)
    sims = []
    for _ in range(BOOT):
        s = [pairs[rng.randrange(len(pairs))] for _ in pairs]
        sims.append(sum(a for _, a in s) / sum(b for b, _ in s))
    sims.sort()
    return ratio, sims[int(0.025 * BOOT)], sims[int(0.975 * BOOT) - 1]


def round_stats(record: dict) -> dict:
    load = lambda rid: {t["task_id"]: t for t in json.loads((RUNS / f"{rid}.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))["tasks"]}  # noqa: E731
    before, after = load(record["before"]), load(record["after"])
    common = sorted(before.keys() & after.keys())
    fixed = sum(not before[k]["passed"] and after[k]["passed"] for k in common)
    broke = sum(before[k]["passed"] and not after[k]["passed"] for k in common)
    tok = lambda t: t["input_tokens"] + t["output_tokens"]  # noqa: E731
    ratio, lo, hi = token_ratio_ci([(tok(before[k]), tok(after[k])) for k in common])
    return {"before": record["before"], "after": record["after"], "kept": record["kept"], "tasks": len(common),
            "fixed": fixed, "broke": broke, "p_passes": round(sign_test(fixed, broke), 4),
            "token_ratio": round(ratio, 3), "ci_low": round(lo, 3), "ci_high": round(hi, 3)}


def all_rounds() -> list[dict]:
    out = []
    for p in sorted(RUNS.glob("*.round.json")):
        r = json.loads(p.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

# Medic

An agent that reads a failing agent's trace, finds the broken step, patches its
config, and proves the fix on tasks it has never seen. The model proposes. The
checks decide.

Two live heals, one on Bedrock in minutes ago, one recorded from Groq in October.
The citation heal rewrote a **system-prompt line**, not a flag, so Medic fixes
more than a boolean.

> **Demo GIF:** _to be recorded_

---

## Results

| Bug | Patient | Status | Before | After | Held-out | Patch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `parse_error` | `nova-micro` | **live** | 2 steps FAIL | 3 steps PASS | 4/4 | one boolean |
| `hallucinated_citation` | `nova-micro` | **live** | 3 steps FAIL | 3 steps PASS | 2/2 | **system_prompt** |
| `loop` | `gpt-oss-20b` (Groq) | historical, Oct 10 2026 | 10 steps FAIL | 6 steps PASS | 2/2 | `system_prompt` |
| `wrong_args` | `nova-micro` | does not reproduce | passes 3/3 | n/a | n/a | n/a |

**The live `parse_error` heal.** Patient `nova-micro`, Medic `claude-sonnet-4.6`,
both AWS Bedrock. The tool returned malformed JSON, the agent had no recovery
path, and the run produced no answer at all.

| | steps | tokens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| before | 2 | 2,020 | **FAIL**, `JSONDecodeError: Illegal trailing comma` |
| after, train | 3 | 4,721 | PASS |
| after, held-out x4 | 3 + 3 + 1 + 1 | 13,426 | PASS |

Medic named the failing span, typed it `parse_error`, scored it **0.95
confidence**, and quoted the error verbatim out of the trace. Nobody told it what
the bug was.

```diff
-retry_on_parse_error: false
+retry_on_parse_error: true
```

**$0.009426 per heal.** Reproduced 3 of 3. Record:
[`evidence/real_heal_loop_parse_error.json`](evidence/real_heal_loop_parse_error.json).

**The live `hallucinated_citation` heal.** Reproduced 3 of 3 on the unmodified
preset. Medic found the exact prompt line that licensed the bug and quoted it
back: *"If you did not fetch a page, you may still cite the URL from the search
result."* The patch replaced it with a fetched-only rule. Train PASS, both
held-out PASS, **$0.016347**:
[`evidence/real_heal_loop_hallucinated_citation.json`](evidence/real_heal_loop_hallucinated_citation.json).

**A cheaper medic, measured.** `claude-haiku` healed `parse_error` with the same
patient, same tasks, identical patient tokens (24,874). Sonnet 1,568 tokens,
**$0.009557** total. Haiku 1,545 tokens, **$0.004419**. That is 68% off the medic
 The Sonnet figure here is a separate run from the headline $0.009426;
 run-to-run variance is about 1%.
share with the patient held fixed:
[`evidence/real_heal_parse_error_haiku_pinned_claude-haiku.json`](evidence/real_heal_parse_error_haiku_pinned_claude-haiku.json).

**The clean gate: 39 of 39.** Unmodified config, `nova-micro`, 13 tasks x 3 runs,
zero misses:
[`evidence/gate_nova_micro_clean.json`](evidence/gate_nova_micro_clean.json). It
failed 4 of 13 the first time, and three of those four were my harness, not the
model.

**Historical, Groq, Oct 10 2026.** `loop` went 10 steps FAIL to 6 steps PASS with
both held-out passing. Groq left the chain because its free tier is 200,000
tokens a day and one take costs about 36,000, which is four takes with no room to
rehearse. Evidence kept and labelled by date:
[`evidence/real_heal_loop.json`](evidence/real_heal_loop.json).

---

## How a heal works

```
failing trace -> diagnose -> surgeon -> patch medic.yaml -> verify
  (neatlogs)     real LLM    real LLM     ONE file         train + held-out
                                            never Python   hard checks
```

1. **Reproduce.** Run the patient on the buggy config. A deterministic check
   decides whether it failed. No LLM opinion involved.
2. **Diagnose.** Send the span tree and the failing check to the LLM. It returns a
   named span, a failure type and a confidence score.
3. **Patch.** The surgeon patches `medic.yaml` only, on a copy, written to the
   real file only with `--apply`.
4. **Verify.** Re-run train, then every held-out task. All must pass or the
   attempt is rejected and Medic retries, up to three times.

**Medic edits exactly one file: `medic.yaml`.** Never Python. Four fields:
`system_prompt`, `tools.<name>.description`, `max_steps`, `retry_on_parse_error`.

---

## Quickstart

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt

cp .env.example .env          # add NEATLOGS_API_KEY and an LLM key
set -a && . ./.env && set +a  # so .env wins over any stale LLM_* in your shell

.venv/bin/python cli.py doctor
.venv/bin/python cli.py run  --bug parse_error --llm real
.venv/bin/python cli.py heal --bug parse_error --llm real
```

Or the wrapper, which loads `.env` and pins the patient so the heal is attributed
to the right model: `bash run.sh before`, then `bash run.sh heal`. Without that
pin both patient and medic fall back to `nova-lite`.

The suites need no key and no network: `.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/ -q`.

**The scripted path cannot heal.** `--llm scripted` works for `run`, `report` and
`reset`, but not `heal`: a scripted model diagnosing a scripted patient would be
grading its own homework. With no key set, `heal` fails loudly and names the
missing variables.

---

## Scope and roadmap

Config-only is a deliberate safety choice, not a limitation of effort: every patch
is small, reviewable as a diff, and reversible by flipping one field back.
Roadmap: tool-description and schema patches, then code patches behind the same
approval and held-out gate, then running on real third-party agent traces pulled
from neatlogs.

---

## Sponsor tools

**neatlogs is the input.** Every span of the failing run is exported and visible
in the dashboard, which is what makes "Medic found the broken step" verifiable
rather than asserted. Medic reads traces back over
`GET /api/traces/v3/<trace-id>` and falls back to a local JSON file when the API
is down, so a heal never dies because a vendor is.

# Pitstop

**An autonomous pit crew for AI agents.** Point Pitstop at an agent repo. It runs
the agent's evals, reads the neatlogs traces of the failing runs, works out the
root cause, patches the code, re-runs the evals, and keeps the patch only if the
numbers improve. Each accepted fix lands as its own git commit with before/after
metrics and trace ids. Patches that don't help are reverted.

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) (Oct 10–12, 2026) by team **4'feetus**.

**First real run** ([report](reports/pitstop-1010-2320-db0d.md)): Scout on `claude-haiku`, Pitstop on `claude-sonnet-4.6`, via the hackathon LiteLLM proxy.

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| tasks passing | 0/6 | **6/6** |
| tokens (6 tasks) | 58,879 | **16,302 (-72%)** |
| est. cost per eval run | $0.0697 | **$0.0251 (-64%)** |
| avg latency | 4.6 s | 3.2 s |

Three rounds, three accepted fixes, each its own commit with the evidence that justified it:

1. **Fenced JSON.** Every neatlogs trace ended in `scout.research status=ERROR JSONDecodeError`; the timelines showed answers starting with a markdown code fence. Pitstop stripped fences before parsing (+19 checks).
2. **Context bloat.** `people_search` returned ~50k chars of full profiles into context. Pitstop trimmed it to name/title (0 → 5 tasks pass).
3. **Invented numbers.** The prompt said "never leave a field null", so the model filled zerodha.com's missing funding with 0. Pitstop allowed null for unknown values (5 → 6).

Pitstop spent $0.21 (7 model calls), read 9 neatlogs traces back and ran 7 Entire Graph searches.

## How it works

```
            ┌──────────── evals (pitstop.toml: eval_cmd) ─────────────┐
            ▼                                                          │
  target agent ──traces──▶ neatlogs ──trace API──▶ evidence ─┬▶ DIAGNOSE (claude-sonnet-4.6)
  target repo ──entire graph search──▶ candidate fix sites ───┘
                                                                       │ ranked root-cause hypotheses
                                                                       ▼
            keep + commit ◀── ACCEPT ◀── compare ◀── evals ◀── tests ◀── PATCH (search/replace edits)
            revert        ◀── REJECT ◀──┘                     │
                                     repair once ◀── edit didn't apply / tests failed
```

1. **Evaluate.** Run the target's eval command (declared in its `pitstop.toml`).
   The harness meters every model call itself, so the agent can't hide steps.
2. **Collect evidence.** For each failing task: failed checks, a step-by-step
   timeline (tool calls, arguments, result sizes, errors, tokens per step) and
   the neatlogs spans and detections for that task's trace, read back through the neatlogs trace API.
3. **Localize.** Each failure signal (an exception, a failing tool call, an
   oversized tool result, an invented value) becomes an `entire graph search`
   over the target repo. Only hits in editable files are kept, as candidate fix sites.
4. **Diagnose.** The model returns ranked hypotheses, each citing evidence
   (task, step, failure text), and sees every earlier attempt and why it was rejected.
5. **Patch.** Minimal search/replace edits, limited to files the target marks
   `editable`. Evals and data are read-only, so the agent can't game its own tests.
   If an edit doesn't apply or the unit tests fail, the error goes back to the
   model for one repair attempt.
6. **Verify.** Re-run the evals. Accept only if more tasks pass, or more checks
   pass, or results stay equal with ≥10% fewer tokens, and no passing task
   regresses. Otherwise revert.
7. **Report.** A markdown + JSON report with the before/after table, every
   accepted diff, every rejected attempt and why, and all trace ids.

Pitstop has a hard USD budget (`--budget`) for its own model calls and stops
cleanly (reverting any half-applied patch) when it hits it.

## The patient: Scout

[`patients/scout`](patients/scout) is a small but real tool-using research agent:
company website in, JSON brief out (headcount, funding, founding year, HQ,
leaders), built on Crustdata company and people data. Its eval checks that the
brief parses, names the right company, matches the data source number for
number (no invented values), lists real people, and stays within a token budget.

Scout ships with the faults real agents ship with. Pitstop isn't told what they are.

## Quick start

```bash
python -m venv .venv && .venv/Scripts/activate      # or source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
cp .env.example .env                                 # add LITELLM_API_KEY and NEATLOGS_API_KEY
pitstop doctor --ping
pitstop init-demo                                    # copies Scout into sandbox/scout as a git repo
pitstop eval                                         # baseline
pitstop heal --rounds 4 --budget 1.50                # the pit stop
```

Offline (no keys, scripted models): `pytest -q`.

### Using it on your own agent

Add a `pitstop.toml` to your agent repo:

```toml
[target]
name = "my-agent"
description = "what it does"
eval_cmd = ["{python}", "-m", "evals.run", "--out", "{out}", "--model", "{model}"]
test_cmd = ["{python}", "-m", "pytest", "-q"]
editable = ["agent/*.py", "agent/prompts.py"]
context  = ["evals/run.py"]
```

Your eval command must write JSON with a `summary` (`tasks`, `passed`,
`total_tokens`, `cost_usd`, `tool_errors`, ...) and per-task `checks`,
`failures`, `steps` and `trace_id`. See [`patients/scout/evals/run.py`](patients/scout/evals/run.py).

## Sponsor tools

| Tool | How Pitstop uses it |
|---|---|
| **neatlogs** | Every Scout run and every Pitstop step is traced (`neatlogs.wrap`, `@neatlogs.span`, `neatlogs.log`). Pitstop reads each failing trace back through the neatlogs trace API (project key: spans, errors, tokens and neatlogs' own detections) as diagnosis evidence. Before/after trace ids go in each commit and report. |
| **Entire** | Inside the agent: Pitstop uses Entire Graph (`entire graph search`) to localize each failure to candidate fix sites before diagnosing. Building the agent: the repo is Entire-enabled for Claude Code (sessions captured as checkpoints linked to commits) and Graph-enabled (`AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` point coding agents at `entire graph search`). |
| **cfo.ai** | Ari (cfo.ai's AI CFO) built Pitstop's 12-month model: pricing, unit economics, forecast, burn, runway and 12 sensitivity scenarios. Headline: $10k runs out in month 3, ~$28.5k bridge needed at $49; don't price Team at $29; $79 breaks even within the year. [Live model](https://cfo.ai/s/W2RB_otvpzPIaBn6) · [`docs/business-plan.md`](docs/business-plan.md) |
| **Crustdata** | Scout's live data source (`SCOUT_DATA=live`). |
| **LiteLLM (hackathon proxy)** | All model calls: `claude-haiku` for Scout, `claude-sonnet-4.6` for Pitstop. |

## Layout

```
src/pitstop/      cli · heal loop · diagnose/patch crew · evidence (neatlogs trace read-back) · target (edits, git) · report
patients/scout/   the patient agent, its evals, fixtures and tests
tests/            offline end-to-end pit stops with scripted models
reports/          reports from real runs
hackathon.md      build log

# Suture

An agent that fixes broken agents, and only hands the fix over once an outside check shows it worked.

Built for neatHack, track "Build an agent that works (literally)".

neatlogs finds what broke and can suggest a fix. Suture tests the fix, and only hands it over once a signed outside check shows it worked.

## What it does

You point Suture at an AI agent that sometimes gets things wrong. Suture then:

1. Runs the outside check (StressProof, 12 probes) on the agent and saves the signed "before" report.
2. Reads the failing runs from the agent's neatlogs traces, so it fixes what actually broke, not what it guesses broke.
3. Asks the model for a patch and applies it to a copy of the agent, never the original.
4. Runs the agent's own tests, plus a new test written from the failure that fails on the original code.
5. Puts the patched copy online and runs StressProof again for the signed "after" report.
6. Keeps the fix only if quiet failures (wrong answers that look fine) are 0 and the score did not drop. Otherwise it throws the patch away and tries again, up to 3 times.
7. If a fix is kept, it opens a pull request. It never merges. A person decides.

## One run you can check

Target: Clerk, a small refund-lookup agent (`targets/clerk`). Its first draft answered broken requests with a confident, made-up answer.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| StressProof score | 75 (PARTIAL) | 92 in the pull request, 100 in the latest re-run |
| Quiet failures | 1 | 0 |
| Attempts used | | 1 of 3 |
| Cost of the fix | | about $0.11 (model about $0.10, two outside checks $0.01) |

The signed reports and the numbers are in `evidence/`. The pull request is [#1](https://github.com/Sireadell/suture/pull/1).

## Try it yourself in one minute

```powershell
python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
pip install -r requirements.txt
copy .env.example .env      # then fill in your own keys
python -m pytest targets\clerk
python -m suture.loop
```

Open any signed report link in `evidence/scorecard.json`. Each one is a StressProof page anyone can verify.

## How it uses the three event tools

| Tool | Use in Suture |
|---|---|
| neatlogs | Suture traces itself and the target agent. It reads failing runs and its own cost back through the neatlogs command line. |
| Entire | Build sessions are recorded as checkpoints on this repo, linked from the submission. |
| cfo.ai | The business plan: price per accepted fix, cost per fix, revenue and runway. Numbers come from the real run above. |

## What existed before the event

StressProof, the outside checker, is my earlier project (github.com/Sireadell/stressproof). Suture calls it as a service. Everything in this repo (the repair loop, the neatlogs reading, the keep rule, Clerk and the other test agents) was written during the event.

## What this is not

- It does not merge anything. It opens a pull request and stops.
- It does not promise a fix every time. If it cannot prove a fix, it hands back nothing and says so.
- It is not a general bug fixer. It repairs one kind of fault, agents that answer bad input with a confident wrong answer.
- It does not prove the target is perfect. A score of 100 means the 12 probes passed, nothing more.
- Today it has one fully proven target. More are in `targets/` and are not claimed until their runs are in `evidence/`.

## Limits I know about

- neatlogs Fixes is not used yet. The command line has no Fixes command, and connecting GitHub in neatlogs did not work for this project.
- The neatlogs login I have is read-only, so Suture cannot write its verdict back into neatlogs.
- neatlogs cost counts leave out the model's thinking tokens, so Suture also keeps its own counters and reports the larger number.

# PatchPilot AI — Autonomous Issue-to-Verified-Fix Agent

[![neatHacks 2026](https://img.shields.io/badge/neatHacks-2026-6366f1.svg)](https://hack.entire.io/neathacks-2026/)
[![Python 3.12+](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.12%20%7C%203.14-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/)
[![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-26%20passed%20%7C%20100%25-brightgreen.svg)]()
[![Observability](https://img.shields.io/badge/Neatlogs-Instrumented-blueviolet.svg)](https://docs.neatlogs.com/)
[![Continuous Memory](https://img.shields.io/badge/Entire-Enabled-black.svg)](https://entire.io/)

> **Autonomous GitHub issue-to-verified-fix agent that investigates bugs, reproduces failures, edits code, runs tests, recovers from failed attempts, and provides verifiable evidence before claiming a fix is complete.**

---

## 🌟 The Core Differentiator: Verified Recovery

Today's generative AI coding tools generate candidate patches quickly, but suffer from **unverified hallucinations and silent regressions**. Over 90% of AI-generated fixes fail because they either break existing features or fail to solve the actual root cause.

**PatchPilot AI never claims success without proof.**

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[GitHub Issue Intake] --> B[Baseline Bug Reproduction]
    B -->|Confirmed Failure| C[Formulate Investigation Plan]
    C --> D[Generate Patch Attempt #N]
    D --> E[Isolated Test Execution]
    E --> F{All Tests Passed?}
    F -->|No: Failure or Regression| G[Failure Classification]
    G --> H[Automated Instant Rollback]
    H --> I[Pivot Strategy & Refine Context]
    I -->|Budget Remaining| D
    I -->|Max Budget Exhausted| J[Report Failed Attempt]
    F -->|Yes: Dual Suites Passed| K[Independent Verification]
    K --> L[Neatlogs & Entire Trace Checkpoint]
    L --> M[Export PR-Ready Evidence Report]
```

---

## 🚀 Key Features

- **Autonomous Issue Intake:** Ingests issues from GitHub URLs, local JSON/Markdown files, or CLI prompts.
- **Baseline Bug Reproduction:** Confirms the bug exists by running the test suite *before* generating code.
- **Controlled Patch Application:** Uses unified diffs with in-memory backups for instant zero-loss rollbacks.
- **Failure Classification:** Analyzes stderr/stdout to distinguish syntax errors, timeouts, assertion failures, and regressions.
- **Regression Shield:** Evaluates both acceptance tests and existing regression suites on every attempt.
- **Neatlogs Observability:** Live workflow-level tracing streamed to Neatlogs ingest (`https://ingest.neatlogs.com/v1/trace`).
- **Entire Continuous Memory:** Tracks agent sessions, commits, and local code graphs using Entire CLI (`v0.11.4`).
- **PR-Ready Reports:** Exports both human-readable Markdown and machine-readable JSON reports. **Never automatically merges code without human review.**

---

# Patient Zero

An app that gets attacked, heals itself, and writes an antibody so the same failure can't come back. Built solo for #neatHack (team: Trace Element).

## How it works
1. **Detect:** attack.py sends malformed requests to a small Flask app. Any 5xx is a crash.
2. **Diagnose:** the healer reads the traceback and source, and Gemini proposes a fix.
3. **Quarantine:** the fix runs on a copy of the app (port 5001).
4. **Verify:** attack.py and pytest must both pass against the copy.
5. **Promote:** only then is the fix copied into the real app. Otherwise it is rejected.
6. **Antibody:** a regression test (tests/test_antibody.py) and a lesson (lessons.json) are saved.

## Result
- Before: 5 attacks crashed the app with a 500 (body was a list, "hello", 123, true or [[1]]).
- After: all 5 return 400, and 8 tests pass.
- Honest gap: `{"name": 123}` still returns 201, because the app stores a number as a name. It does not crash, so the healer did not cover it.

## How we used the required tools
- **neatlogs:** every heal run is traced with spans detect, diagnose, quarantine, verify and promote. See docs/neatlogs-*.png.
- **Entire:** the whole build is recorded as checkpoints (OpenCode sessions linked to commits). See docs/entire-*.png.
- **cfo.ai:** a business plan for Patient Zero (price, costs, revenue, runway). See docs/cfo-*.png. Price ($49 per protected app per month) and cost per heal are assumptions, not measurements.
  Runway if revenue stopped: base case 17.1 months before a founder salary and 6.3 after, growth case 13.9 and 5.0.

## Evidence
- Business plan: docs/cfo-1-runway-stress-test.png, cfo-2-runway-table.png, cfo-3-scenarios.png, cfo-4-assumptions.png
- Entire: docs/entire-1-checkpoints.png and the other entire-*.png files
- neatlogs traces: docs/neatlogs-*.png
- Before-fix evidence: evidence/ folder
- Built in public: [PASTE YOUR #neatHack POST LINKS HERE]
- Demo video: [PASTE VIDEO LINK HERE]

## Run it
pip install -r requirements.txt, add GEMINI_API_KEY and NEATLOGS_API_KEY to .env, then run python heal.py.

# TraceHealer

> **Failure trace → reproduced bug → repository context → minimal patch → sandbox verification → review-ready draft**

TraceHealer is an autonomous incident-response system for production AI agents. It turns structured runtime evidence into a tested software change while keeping publication and merge behind explicit safety gates.

The included neatHack scenario is fully executable: Order API v3 moves a customer email field, a support agent crashes and retries three times, and TraceHealer reproduces the failure, repairs the target in an isolated workspace, runs four regressions, commits the verified fix locally, persists the evidence, and optionally delivers a draft GitHub PR and after-trace.

## Complete working flow

1. **Intake** — native TraceHealer JSON, wrapped neatlogs events, or OTLP JSON enters through a validated API/webhook.
2. **Reproduce** — the target repository fixture is copied to a unique workspace; the original tests and failed production replay must fail as expected.
3. **Diagnose** — TraceHealer selects the actionable error span, classifies it, extracts the stack frame, and builds a local repository context graph.
4. **Patch** — a one-file compatibility repair is applied to the isolated checkout.
5. **Verify** — the exact failed payload, legacy contract, current contract, and typed-error behavior run through `node --test`.
6. **Commit** — only a green repair is committed in the workspace; a real git patch and machine-readable report are saved.
7. **Persist** — the run, logs, metrics, context, commit, delivery state, and artifact paths are atomically recorded.
8. **Deliver** — when configured, TraceHealer exports the verified run, sends Slack evidence, and creates a **draft** GitHub PR. It never merges.

No secret is required for steps 1–7.

## Features

- Production-style control center, incident queue, trace waterfall, diagnosis, diff review, healing runs, run detail, evaluations, repositories, and integration pages
- Server-driven progress: async run creation plus polling of real persisted lifecycle states
- Explicit run state machine, append-only audit events, idempotency, cancellation, timeouts, and stale-run recovery
- Deterministic classifiers for schema drift, malformed JSON, timeouts, rate limits, and unknown application errors
- Native and OTLP trace normalization with runtime validation
- HMAC-SHA256 webhook authentication
- Actual before/after subprocess execution with timeouts and bounded logs
- Failure-reproduction gate and four executable regressions
- Local repository graph and impacted-test discovery
- Generated patch and JSON report download endpoints
- Filesystem audit store with atomic writes and run retrieval APIs
- Automatic or manual draft-PR delivery after verification
- Optional after-trace export and Slack notifications
- Secret-safe integration readiness endpoint
- Docker production image, persistent volume, healthcheck, CI, security headers, tests, and responsive UI

## Quick start

```bash
npm install --legacy-peer-deps
cp .env.example .env.local
npm run dev
```

Open [http://localhost:3000](http://localhost:3000), inspect the red span, and click **Heal incident**. The server performs the real reproduce/patch/test/commit pipeline and exposes the resulting patch and verification artifacts in the UI.

```bash
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build
```

## Docker

```bash
cp .env.example .env
# Add optional integration secrets.
docker compose up --build
```

Runtime evidence is stored in the `tracehealer-data` volume. See [`docs/OPERATIONS.md`](docs/OPERATIONS.md).

# Ouroboros

**An agent that eats its own execution traces to get cheaper without getting wrong.**

Built for [neatHack](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon), October 2026.

---

## The result

Both benchmark tasks start from a **genuinely failing** test suite, and the run takes
them to passing. Same task, same objective verifier, one strategy change in between:

```
metric        baseline  improved  delta
------------  --------  --------  ---------------
total tokens  7479      2412      -5067 (-67.75%)
task passed   True      True

verdict: CHEAPER AND STILL CORRECT
```

**67.75% fewer tokens on a real task, which still passes.** The task did not change.
Only how the agent worked changed.

A second task in a different domain (text slug handling rather than arithmetic)
reproduces it, which is what shows the mechanism generalises rather than fitting one
fixture:

```
metric        baseline  improved  delta
------------  --------  --------  ---------------
total tokens  6531      2408      -4123 (-63.13%)
task passed   True      True
```

**These figures are produced by CI on every push**, not pasted from a local run, so
they cannot quietly drift: `.github/workflows/ouroboros.yml` runs both tasks and
prints the before and after into the job log where anyone can read them.

### What the numbers do and do not say

They do say: on both tasks, a strategy chosen from the agent's own trace cut total
tokens by roughly two thirds while an independent verifier still confirmed the suite
passes, and a change that stopped it passing was reverted rather than shipped.

They do not say: that the agent invented the fix. The offline demonstration replays a
scripted plan, so the arithmetic of the comparison is about **strategy efficiency
given a plan**, not about search or reasoning. The plan is the same in both runs;
only the strategy differs. Running against a live model is supported
(`OUROBOROS_API_KEY`, `OUROBOROS_MODEL`) and is where the reasoning claim would be
made.

Reproduce either one in a single command, with no API key and no network:

```bash
pip install -e .
ouroboros improve --task bench/task_demo  --offline --cycles 2
ouroboros improve --task bench/task_demo2 --offline --cycles 2
```

The next cycle is the interesting one. Cycle 1 proposes another change, the
independent verifier refuses to confirm the task, and **the agent reverts it and
writes the reason to memory**:

```
cycle 0: applying 3 change(s)
cycle 0: KEPT, 2412 tokens (5067 fewer than baseline), task still passes
cycle 1: applying 1 change(s)
cycle 1: REVERTED, task no longer confirmed or no gain

# Ouroboros

An agent pipeline that watches itself die, then fixes itself.

**neatHack 2026 project (team *um*, solo build).** Built for the "Build an agent that works (literally)" track.

## The idea

Most agent demos show the happy path. Ouroboros treats failure as the feature:

1. **Worker** (`ouro/worker/dossier.py`) — given a company domain, it plans, calls Crustdata tools (identify → enrich → people → web search), and synthesizes a verified company dossier. Every LLM call, tool call, and failure is traced in **neatlogs**.
2. **Supervisor** (`ouro/supervisor/heal.py`) — reads the worker's run log and its *own* neatlogs traces, classifies each failure (429s, invalid tool args, verification gaps), picks a remediation, re-runs, and verifies the fix.
3. **Watch daemon** (`ouro watch`) — keeps polling the run log in the background; every *new* failure is healed exactly once and recorded in `state/watch_state.json`. This is the "watch a running system" pattern: the agent doesn't need a human to press the fix button.

The judges' hard-to-fake evidence — *a run where an action failed, showing what the agent did next* — is the product itself.

## Docs

- `hackathon.md` — the build log (dated entries, evidence links)
- `docs/business-plan.md` — cfo.ai unit economics, pricing, runway (numbers pulled from trace costs)
- `docs/demo-script.md` — 3-minute demo narration and recording checklist
- `docs/submission.md` — judging-criteria evidence map and pre-submission gates

## Layout

```
ouro/
├── worker/dossier.py     # dossier agent: plan -> tools -> synthesize -> verify
├── supervisor/heal.py    # trace/run-log reader, failure classifier, remediation
├── tools/crustdata.py    # Crustdata API client (with optional fault injection)
├── state.py              # JSONL run log (state across runs)
└── trace.py              # neatlogs init/shutdown
```

## Setup

```bash
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]"
cp .env.example .env   # fill in keys
```

Env vars:

| Var | Where from |
|---|---|
| `CRUSTDATA_API_KEY` | Crustdata dashboard (hackathon promo code `NEATLOGS-OCT2026`) |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | OpenAI |
| `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` | app.neatlogs.com → Settings → API keys → **top** key (Project API key, not the `nlw_` ingest key) |

Optional: `OURO_MODEL` (default `gpt-4o`), `OURO_FAULT_INJECT=1` (deterministic first-call 429 per endpoint, for repeatable demo runs), `OURO_MOCK=1` (offline fakes, no keys needed).

## Usage

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m ouro doctor                       # keys + neatlogs probe + crustdata endpoint access
.venv/bin/python -m ouro run crustdata.com            # one dossier (traced)
.venv/bin/python -m ouro batch a.com,b.com            # batch, state across runs
.venv/bin/python -m ouro runs                         # run log summary
.venv/bin/python -m ouro supervise --window-hours 24   # classify failures, remediate, rerun, compare
.venv/bin/python -m ouro watch --once                 # one background healing cycle
.venv/bin/python -m ouro watch --interval 300         # poll every 5 minutes, heal each new failure once
```

Outputs land in `out/<domain>/<run_id>/` (`dossier.json`, `run.json`); the run log is `state/runs.jsonl`.

### Offline demo (no keys, no network)

"""Docs Bisect. Find the release of a package that broke one runbook step.

Every probe replays stored commands in a fresh container with PIP_CONSTRAINT pinning one
release. No model call happens here. A test enforces that this file imports no model module.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import re
import subprocess
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from typing import Any, Callable

import neatlogs

from firstrun import config, state as state_io
from firstrun.models import FileSpec, Runbook, Step
from firstrun.tracing import mark_error, set_io

CONSTRAINTS_PATH = "/tmp/constraints.txt"
PYPI_URL = "https://pypi.org/pypi/{package}/json"


# --- releases ----------------------------------------------------------------

def _fetch_json(url: str) -> dict:
    """GET a JSON document. Falls back to curl when Python's CA store cannot verify the host."""
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=30) as resp:
            return json.loads(resp.read().decode("utf-8"))
    except Exception:  # noqa: BLE001 - an expired CA root or a proxy: try curl once
        proc = subprocess.run(["curl", "-sSfL", url], capture_output=True, timeout=60)
        if proc.returncode != 0:
            raise RuntimeError(f"cannot fetch {url}: {proc.stderr.decode('utf-8', 'replace').strip()[:200]}")
        return json.loads(proc.stdout.decode("utf-8"))


def _allows_python(requires_python: str | None, python: str) -> bool:
    if not requires_python:
        return True
    from packaging.specifiers import InvalidSpecifier, SpecifierSet

    try:
        spec = SpecifierSet(requires_python)
    except InvalidSpecifier:
        return True
    # "3.11" means the newest 3.11 patch release, which the slim image ships.
    return spec.contains(f"{python}.99", prereleases=True)


def releases(package: str, python: str = "3.11",
             fetch: Callable[[str], dict] | None = None) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """(version, upload_date) for each final release, oldest to newest, that allows `python`."""
    from packaging.version import InvalidVersion, Version

    data = (fetch or _fetch_json)(PYPI_URL.format(package=package))
    found: list[tuple[Version, str, str]] = []
    for ver, files in (data.get("releases") or {}).items():
        try:
            parsed = Version(ver)
        except InvalidVersion:
            continue
        if parsed.is_prerelease or parsed.is_devrelease or not files:
            continue
        live = [f for f in files if not f.get("yanked")]
        if not live:
            continue
        if not any(_allows_python(f.get("requires_python"), python) for f in live):
            continue
        stamps = sorted(f.get("upload_time_iso_8601") or f.get("upload_time") or "" for f in live)
        found.append((parsed, ver, stamps[0][:10]))
    found.sort(key=lambda t: t[0])
    return [(ver, date) for _, ver, date in found]


# --- slicing -----------------------------------------------------------------

def _name_pattern(package: str) -> re.Pattern[str]:
    parts = re.split(r"[-_.]+", package.lower())
    return re.compile(r"(?<![A-Za-z0-9])" + r"[-_.]?".join(map(re.escape, parts)) + r"(?![A-Za-z0-9])", re.I)


def slice_steps(runbook: Runbook, failing_step_id: int, package: str,
                patches: list | None = None) -> list[Step]:
    """The minimal steps for one probe, in runbook order, ending with the failing step.

    Other steps use their patched command (environment fixes stay). The failing step keeps its original command.
    """
    from firstrun.verify import apply_patches

    patched = apply_patches(runbook, patches or [])
    originals = {s.id: s for s in runbook.steps}
    if failing_step_id not in originals:
        raise ValueError(f"no step {failing_step_id} in the runbook")
    failing = originals[failing_step_id]
    pattern = _name_pattern(package)
    out: list[Step] = []
    for step in patched.steps:
        if step.id > failing_step_id or step.skipped_out_of_scope:
            continue
        if step.id == failing_step_id:
            out.append(failing.model_copy(deep=True))
            continue
        mentions = bool(pattern.search(step.command))
        makes_file = any(f.path.rsplit("/", 1)[-1] in failing.command for f in step.files)
        if mentions or makes_file:
            out.append(step)
    return out


# --- one probe ---------------------------------------------------------------

def _default_factory(image: str, name: str, env: dict[str, str]):
    from firstrun.sandbox import Container, _allowlist_env

    return Container(image=image, name=name, env={**_allowlist_env(), **env})


def _default_run_step(container, step):
    from firstrun.executor import run_step

    return run_step(container, step)


_BOX = "╭╮╯╰│─┌┐└┘├┤┬┴┼ "


def _error_line(result) -> str:
    """The most telling line of a failed step: the last one that names an error, else the last line.

    Rich prints errors inside a box, so the box characters are stripped first.
    """
    for text in (result.stderr, result.stdout):
        lines = [ln.strip(_BOX).strip() for ln in text.splitlines()]
        lines = [re.sub(r"^/tmp/\.fr_step\.sh: line \d+: ", "", ln) for ln in lines if ln.strip(_BOX).strip()]
        if lines:
            named = [ln for ln in lines if re.search(r"error|no such|not found|invalid|unrecognized|failed", ln, re.I)]
            return (named or lines)[-1][:120]
    return "timed out" if result.timed_out else f"exit {result.exit_code}"


def probe(steps: list[Step], image: str, package: str, version: str,
          container_factory: Callable[..., Any] | None = None,
          run_step: Callable[[Any, Step], Any] | None = None) -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """TOOL span `probe.<version>`. Run `steps` in a fresh container with `package` pinned to `version`.

    The last step is the one under test. Returns (passed, short error line). Never calls a model.
    `container_factory(image, name, env)` returns a context manager.
    """
    factory = container_factory or _default_factory
    runner = run_step or _default_run_step
    name = f"firstrun-bisect-{package}-{version}"
    env = {"PIP_CONSTRAINT": CONSTRAINTS_PATH}
    passed, error = False, ""
    with neatlogs.trace(f"probe.{version}", kind="TOOL") as span, config.block_model_calls():
        span.set_attribute("package", package)
        span.set_attribute("version", version)
        try:
            with factory(image, name, env) as container:
                container.write_files([FileSpec(path=CONSTRAINTS_PATH, content=f"{package}=={version}\n")])
                passed = True
                for step in steps:
                    result = runner(container, step)
                    if not result.passed:
                        passed = False
                        error = _error_line(result)
                        if step is not steps[-1]:
                            error = f"step {step.id}: {error}"
                        break
        except config.ModelCallBlocked as exc:
            passed, error = False, f"model call blocked: {exc}"
        except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001 - a broken container is a failed probe, not a crash
            if exc.__class__.__name__ == "DockerUnavailable":
                raise
            passed, error = False, f"probe error: {exc}"[:120]
        span.set_attribute("passed", passed)
        set_io(span, input={"package": package, "version": version, "steps": [s.id for s in steps]},
               output={"passed": passed, "error": error})
        if not passed:
            mark_error(span, error)
    return passed, error


# --- the search --------------------------------------------------------------

def _now() -> str:
    return datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat(timespec="seconds")


def bisect_path(run_id: str):
    return state_io.run_dir(run_id) / "bisect.json"


def _save(run_id: str, doc: dict) -> None:
    state_io._write(bisect_path(run_id), json.dumps(doc, indent=2, ensure_ascii=False))


def run(run_id: str, package: str, step_id: int | None = None, max_probes: int = 8,
        container_factory: Callable[..., Any] | None = None,
        run_step: Callable[[Any, Step], Any] | None = None,
        release_list: list[tuple[str, str]] | None = None,
        on_probe: Callable[[dict], None] | None = None) -> dict:
    """WORKFLOW span `firstrun.bisect`. Binary-search the releases of `package` for the first bad one."""
    from firstrun.report import reported_failed_step

    state = state_io.load_state(run_id)
    runbook = state_io.load_runbook(run_id)
    if step_id is None:
        step_id = reported_failed_step(state)
    if step_id is None:
        raise ValueError("this run has no failed step. Pass --step N")
    steps = slice_steps(runbook, step_id, package, state.patches)
    command = next(s.command for s in runbook.steps if s.id == step_id)
    found = re.search(r"python:(\d+\.\d+)", runbook.image)
    python = found.group(1) if found else "3.11"
    doc: dict = {
        "package": package, "step_id": step_id, "command": command, "image": runbook.image,
        "releases_tested": [], "last_good": None, "first_bad": None, "first_bad_date": None,
        "verdict": "", "probes": 0, "started_at": _now(), "finished_at": "",
    }

    from firstrun.tracing import session_attrs

    with neatlogs.trace("firstrun.bisect", kind="WORKFLOW", run_id=run_id, package=package, step_id=step_id,
                        **session_attrs(state_io.target_name(runbook.source_url), "bisect", package=package)
                        ) as root, config.block_model_calls():
        set_io(root, input={"run_id": run_id, "package": package, "step_id": step_id, "max_probes": max_probes})
        rels = release_list if release_list is not None else releases(package, python)
        doc["releases_available"] = len(rels)

        def test(idx: int) -> bool:
            ver, date = rels[idx]
            ok, err = probe(steps, runbook.image, package, ver, container_factory, run_step)
            entry = {"version": ver, "date": date, "passed": ok, "error": err}
            doc["releases_tested"].append(entry)
            doc["probes"] = len(doc["releases_tested"])
            neatlogs.log("probe {version}: {result}", version=ver, result="pass" if ok else "fail", error=err)
            _save(run_id, doc)
            if on_probe:
                on_probe(entry)
            return ok

        def finish(verdict: str) -> dict:
            doc["verdict"] = verdict
            doc["finished_at"] = _now()
            _save(run_id, doc)
            set_io(root, output={k: doc[k] for k in ("last_good", "first_bad", "first_bad_date", "verdict", "probes")})
            return doc

        if len(rels) < 2:
            return finish(f"only {len(rels)} release(s) allow Python {python}: nothing to bisect")
        _save(run_id, doc)
        lo, hi = 0, len(rels) - 1
        newest_ok = test(hi)
        oldest_ok = test(lo)
        if not newest_ok and not oldest_ok:
            return finish("fails on every release: not a version regression")
        if newest_ok and oldest_ok:
            return finish("passes on every release: no regression to find")
        if newest_ok:
            return finish("fails on old releases and passes on new ones: fixed upstream, not broken")
        while hi - lo > 1 and doc["probes"] < max_probes:
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if test(mid):
                lo = mid
            else:
                hi = mid
        doc["last_good"] = rels[lo][0]
        if hi - lo == 1:
            doc["first_bad"], doc["first_bad_date"] = rels[hi]
            return finish(f"first bad release: {package} {rels[hi][0]} ({rels[hi][1]})")
        return finish(f"max probes reached: first bad release is after {rels[lo][0]} and no later than {rels[hi][0]}")

# FirstRun ### Docs that work. Literally. FirstRun runs your quickstart in a clean container, finds the first step that breaks, and proves the fix with a second clean run. [![Live site](https://img.shields.io/badge/site-firstrun.atharvashah.com-0A66D6?style=for-the-badge)](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/) [![neatHack 2026](https://img.shields.io/badge/built%20for-%23neatHack%202026-111111?style=for-the-badge)](https://neatlogs.com/hackathon) [![Tests](https://img.shields.io/badge/tests-295%20offline-1B8A3A?style=for-the-badge)](.github) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.11%2B-3776AB?style=for-the-badge&logo=python&logoColor=white)](pyproject.toml) [**Watch the 3-minute demo**](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JJNWWhSV9pc) · [**Try it in the browser**](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/) · [**Watch a real run**](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/run.html) · [**See the 4 upstream PRs**](#firstrun-found-4-real-docs-bugs-and-opened-4-upstream-prs) · [**Follow the build on X**](https://x.com/cultist_dev)
The 44-second launch film. The video does not play for you? [Open it on the site](https://firstrun.atharvashah.com/) or [download the MP4](docs/assets/firstrun-launch.mp4).

```bash pip install git+https://github.com/HighnessAtharva/firstrun firstrun https://docs.example.com/quickstart ``` ## Break, Fix, Prove Takes 195 Seconds

1. Read
FirstRun reads the page and plans one step per command.
2. Run
Every step runs in a clean container, like a new developer. The first failure stops the run.
3. Prove
A fix is done only when a second clean container passes the whole quickstart.
The input below is a known-broken test fixture (`tests/fixtures/docs/broken_quickstart_FIXTURE.md`), not a real project's docs. Step 3 pins an old chromadb that cannot install on Python 3.11. ```text Step 3 of 4: pip install chromadb==0.3 ERROR: No matching distribution found for numpy~=1.21.6 Cause: docs_bug (source: jev) Patch: step 3 -> pip install chromadb Verified: 4/4 steps passed in a fresh container Time to first success: 195 s ``` FirstRun writes `report.md`, `patch.diff` and `pr_body.md` into the run folder. The patch is one line. ## Seven Teams Get a Different Job Out of the Same Engine | # | You are | The problem | Run this | You get | |---|---|---|---|---| | **1** | A DevRel or docs lead | Nobody tests the quickstart after launch day | `firstrun ` | A pass or a verified fix, with a PR draft | | **2** | A release manager | A new release of your package broke the docs and you do not know which one | `firstrun bisect --package ` | The last good and first bad release | | **3** | A technical writer | The docs assume tools the reader does not have | `firstrun prereqs ` | A Prerequisites block, proven in a clean container | | **4** | An open-source contributor | You want a first PR that a maintainer merges | `firstrun pr ` | The `gh` commands for the docs PR, source check included | | **5** | An engineer picking a tool | You want to know if the vendor's quickstart works before you commit | `firstrun ` | A time to first success and the first step that breaks | | **6** | A coding agent | You need a loop that checks its own docs work | `firstrun run --resume ` | State after every step and a model-free verify | | **7** | A head of docs | Hundreds of pages, and the code moved under some of them | `firstrun audit owner/repo` | Stale pages with the commits behind them, features with no docs, proposal cards and drafted release notes |
7. Which docs did the product outgrow? Audit the whole docs set from the git history. ```bash firstrun audit fastapi/typer ``` ```bash firstrun audit dbt-labs/dbt-core --docs-repo dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com ``` One blobless clone gives the whole history. The audit then works offline and costs $0 in model calls. Jev sorts commits with no conventional prefix when `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` is set, and every audit is one neatlogs trace. - **Oldest first.** Every page, ranked by the date of its last edit. - **Stale or quiet.** A page is stale when product commits on its topic landed after its last edit, and the report names those commits. An old page that nothing changed under is quiet, so the team can leave it alone. - **Features with no docs.** Each user-facing commit in 120 days is checked against the docs text. A flag or name that no page mentions becomes a "Document this" card. - **Proposal cards.** Document this, refresh this page, feature this, create content around a feature with 3 or more commits, and automate the release notes. - **Drafts.** Release notes for the newest stable tag and up to 3 product highlights, written from commit subjects and pull request numbers. `firstrun audit-issue` turns the newest audit into `issue.md`, one checkbox per card, and prints the `gh issue create` command. It opens nothing on its own. To audit every week, copy [`examples/github-action/firstrun-audit.yml`](examples/github-action/firstrun-audit.yml) into `.github/workflows/`. Each Monday it audits the repo and updates one issue labeled `firstrun-audit`, so the docs team gets a fresh work list without anyone running a command. `--docs-repo` reads the docs from a second repo when the docs site lives apart from the code. Inside this repo, each audit is published to `docs/audits/` and opens at [audit.html](https://1run.netlify.app/audit.html).
1. Does my quickstart work today? Run it every night.
A DevRel team ships a quickstart once and a dependency moves the week after. The first person to find the break is a new user, and most new users leave instead of filing a bug. ```bash firstrun https://docs.example.com/quickstart ``` ## FirstRun Found 4 Real Docs Bugs and Opened 4 Upstream PRs FirstRun ran five open-source quickstarts whose docs live in public repos. Every finding came from a verified run, where a second clean container passed with the fix.

dbt-labs/docs.getdbt.com#10150

# dsh-culprit · 回归归因

> 「这段代码是哪次提交改挂的？」

给一条**有 bug 就退出非零**的命令，dsh-culprit 在仓库历史里二分，直接告诉你肇事提交是哪一个，
并附上它的 diff、改了哪些文件、以及每一步的判定证据。

它不是"再跑一遍测试"，是**把测试变红这件事本身当成一个可以追溯的事实**。

**仓库**：[github.com/ca610/dsh-culprit](https://github.com/ca610/dsh-culprit) · MIT

---

## 为什么需要它

生态里的最近邻是 [`slow-stack/euthyna`](https://github.com/slow-stack/euthyna)：它能按行/按历史回答
"这一行是谁引进的"（`--origins`），那是**历史归因**——它读历史，不执行任何东西。

dsh-culprit 回答的是另一个问题：**"从哪个提交开始，这个行为坏了？"**
它必须真的在那些提交上把命令跑一遍。历史归因猜不到"这一版依赖装不上"、
"这个 commit 的测试超时"、"这个改动只在运行时才炸"。

代价是它**会 checkout 你的工作树**，所以这个插件在工程上有一半的力气都花在
"怎么才能不伤到你"上（见下面的[安全保证](#安全保证)）。

---

## 安装

先拿到代码：

```
git clone https://github.com/ca610/dsh-culprit
```

**常规路径**（用户自管 profile）——由 agent 调用插件管理器：

```
plugin_manager(action: "install_bundle", target: "C:\\path\\to\\dsh-culprit")
```

装完需要重启 profile，宿主才会加载新的 JS。卸载用 `remove_bundle`。

**Windows 桌面版**要绕一下：`desktop` profile 由 Electron 应用独占管理，
`dsh plugin --profile desktop add` 会被 `rejectElectronProfile()` 直接拒掉

# culprit

When a Claude Code task fails, culprit tells you which layer to change: your prompt, your environment,
your agent setup (CLAUDE.md, rules, skills), the harness (tools, MCP, settings, context) or the model.
It re-runs the task with one layer changed at a time. A layer is the cause only if its runs pass
clearly more often than unchanged runs (10 each, one-sided Fisher exact test, p < 0.05). No model
guesses the cause.

## How it decides

1. **Triage.** Your logs (`~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl`) are split into episodes: one prompt and
   everything until your next prompt. Episodes are ranked by interrupts, tool errors, compactions and
   slow turns. A prompt that is only a slash command (`/compact`, `/model opus`) is never a candidate.
   Episodes that can't be replayed are listed last, with the reason.
2. **Confirm.** You say what went wrong (`stopped-short`, `wrong-result`, `ignored-instructions`,
   `wasteful` or `no-failure`) and approve a drafted success criterion.
3. **Baseline.** The episode's starting files are rebuilt in a throwaway copy and the episode is
   replayed unchanged 10 times. A follow-up prompt ("now do it on main") is replayed with its session's
   earlier conversation in place, so Claude knows what "it" is. If 6 or more pass, the failure was luck (**not-reproducible**).
4. **Oracles.** The episode is replayed with one layer improved at a time, cheapest first:

   | Change | Verdict if it now passes |
   |---|---|
   | prompt restated clearly | **task**: change how you ask |
   | your fix script runs first | **environment**: fix the repo or infrastructure |
   | better standing instructions | **agent-setup**: change CLAUDE.md, rules, skills |
   | all tools, relevant files preloaded, double budget | **harness**: change tools, MCP, settings |
   | Fable at max effort instead of the original model | **model**: raise the effort, or change or route the model |

   The restated prompt and the standing instructions are drafted by a model that sees only what the agent
   could have known before the episode began. For a follow-up, the prompt drafter also sees the session's
   earlier prompts and replies (not tool output). The instructions drafter sees the CLAUDE.md files (and
   rules and imports) Claude Code loads at launch, read from the starting copy for the project, plus its
   top-level folder layout, and writes rules that fill their gaps. They are tested the way you would apply
   them: appended to the project's `CLAUDE.md` in the throwaway copy (never your project). The drafter also
   suggests where they belong (project `CLAUDE.md`, `CLAUDE.local.md`, a path-scoped rule, your user
   `CLAUDE.md` or managed policy); the report shows that as an untested suggestion beside the verdict.

   Replays keep the effort level the episode logged. When Fable at max effort passes, two cheaper fixes are
   replayed too: the original model at max effort, and the latest model of the episode's own family (`opus`,
   `sonnet`, `haiku`) at its original effort. The model verdict names every one that passed, cheapest first:
   "raise effort (original model at max effort passed 7/10)", "upgrade to the latest opus (claude-opus-5-5
   passed 8/10)", or "needs Fable (…)" when neither did. An episode already on what `fable` means today (resolved for free and kept a day in
   `runs/models.json`) is tested at max effort only if it ran lower; one on an older Fable is tested as usual.

# Culpritly landing page

Static pre-sell landing page for Culpritly, built for GitHub Pages.

Plain HTML and CSS. No build step, no frameworks, no trackers. The only script is a few lines inline in `404.html`.

## Files

```
index.html            Landing page (with SoftwareApplication + FAQPage JSON-LD)
privacy.html          Privacy page
404.html              Not found page, fully self-contained (inline CSS and logo)
assets/css/style.css  All styles (dark by default, light via prefers-color-scheme)
assets/img/           Logo mark, favicon, Open Graph image
robots.txt            Allows all crawlers, points to the sitemap
sitemap.xml           Home and privacy URLs
.nojekyll             Tells GitHub Pages to serve files as they are
```

## Works at a subpath or at a domain root

All internal links and asset paths are relative (`assets/...`, `privacy.html`, `./`), so the site works both:

- from a GitHub Pages project path, for example `https://faisalalvi.com/culpritly/` or `https://<user>.github.io/culpritly-site/`, and
- later at the root of `https://culpritly.com/`.

`404.html` does not load any external stylesheet or image from the site, because GitHub Pages serves it for missing URLs at any depth, where relative paths would break. A small inline script points its "home" links at `/` on culpritly.com and at the project folder (for example `/culpritly/`) everywh

The canonical URL, `og:url`, `og:image`, `twitter:image`, sitemap and JSON-LD URLs intentionally stay absolute on `https://culpritly.com/`. They become correct as soon as the domain is live.

## Preview locally

From this folder:

```sh
python3 -m http.server 8080
```

Then open http://localhost:8080. Stop the server with Ctrl+C.

# Tracewise

An on-call agent that runs without anyone watching. When something breaks in a running system,
Tracewise works out what broke and why, fixes it itself, checks that the system really recovered,
and writes up the incident with the evidence behind each conclusion. Every resolved incident
becomes memory for the next one.

## How it works

```
Shopfront (7 services) ──telemetry, deploys──▶ Tracewise API ──▶ Postgres
      ▲                                              │
      │ rollback / flags / restart                   ▼
      └──────────────── agent worker ◀──── detector (opens incidents)
                         plan → investigate → hypothesize → act → verify → resolve
```

- **Shopfront** (`demo/`): a small store: gateway, checkout, payments, bank, catalog,
  inventory and orders. Each service reports request metrics, error logs and calls to other
  services every 2 seconds. A deployer runs every service at a chosen git commit and keeps the
  deploy history; a traffic generator keeps it busy.
- **Detector** (`backend/tracewise/detector.py`): compares each service with its own
  15-minute baseline (error rate, p95 latency, silence) with no hand-set thresholds. Unhealthy
  services that are connected are grouped into one incident.
- **Agent** (`backend/tracewise/agent/`): Claude (Opus 5.5) in a tool loop. Read-only tools
  investigate (health, metrics, logs, dependencies, deploys, commits, code, memory); action tools
  change the system (feature flag, rollback, restart); `verify_recovery` watches the services
  until they stay healthy. It can't resolve without a passing verification.
- **Reliability:** the conversation is saved after every turn and incidents are held by a
  renewable lease, so if a worker dies another picks up the run where it stopped. Actions are
  keyed per tool call, so a resumed run never applies one twice. Budgets cap turns, cost and
  actions, and the agent must verify each action before taking another.
- **Changes during an incident** (new deploys, newly affected services) are passed to the agent
  as `[environment update]` messages, and it re-plans.

## Connected coding agents (fix forward)

A rollback stops the bleeding but throws away the feature. Teams connect their own coding agent
and Tracewise hands it the fix:

1. **Connect an account** (`POST /v1/connections`): **Claude** with an Anthropic API key from the
   Claude Console, or **Cursor** with a Cursor API key. Keys are encrypted at rest
   (`TW_SECRET_KEY`), and the runner checks each one with its provider. Claude connects through
   an API key rather than a claude.ai login, because Anthropic doesn't allow third-party products
   to offer claude.ai login or subscription limits.

# Night Shift

**The on-call engineer for your AI agents.** Built for neatHack 2026.

It stops the bleeding by itself, and only wakes you for decisions that can't be undone.

**Live:** https://web-emrq.vercel.app · sign in with GitHub · [SDK docs](https://web-emrq.vercel.app/docs) ·
[sandbox demo, no account needed](https://web-emrq.vercel.app/sandbox)

At 3 AM, a "harmless" change to a production AI agent starts failing. Maybe it pays refunds it
shouldn't, or reads docs from a folder that doesn't exist yet. Every request still returns HTTP 200.
Night Shift notices from the agent's neatlogs traces and the outcomes the agent reports. It then
investigates like a senior SRE: traces, deploy log, diff, and the **Entire checkpoint with the prompt
the coding agent was given**. It prices the damage with the **cfo.ai** unit economics, applies the
reversible fix your policy pre-approves, and proves the fix by having your agent replay the failed
runs. Then it pages you once: *handled, here's what it cost, and a permanent fix is waiting for your
approval in Slack.*

> reproducible; the Scout incidents ran live through the product.

# Trace-Driven Agent Improver

A hackathon MVP that observes a task agent, classifies failures, applies bounded improvements, and promotes a candidate only when benchmark evidence supports it.

## Current scope

- Synthetic support-ticket routing task.
- Two real baseline failure classes: wrong action selection and missing verification.
- Separate development and held-out benchmark splits.
- Local structured trace events plus optional Neatlogs spans.
- Bounded improvement proposals and a promotion/rejection gate.
- CLI and FastAPI endpoints.

The current student agent is deterministic. Neatlogs integration makes its workflow and evaluation outcomes observable; it does not imply that this version uses an LLM or proves general self-improvement.

## Setup

Requires Python 3.11+.

\`\`\`bash
python -m venv .venv
# Windows PowerShell: .venv\\Scripts\\Activate.ps1
# macOS/Linux: source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
\`\`\`

Copy .env.example to .env and set NEATLOGS_API_KEY to the project key from your Neatlogs dashboard. Do not commit .env. If the key is absent, the app and tests run locally without exporting traces.

## Run

\`\`\`bash
python -m pytest -q
python -m app.cli
uvicorn app.main:app --reload
\`\`\`

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs. Call POST /improve to run a complete benchmark and improvement cycle. With a valid NEATLOGS_API_KEY, each benchmark case is exported as a workflow trace with nested action-selection, tool-execution, and verification spans. Check the Neatlogs dashboard for the trace-d

## Improvement loop

Benchmark → Student agent → trace/evaluate → classify failures → propose bounded change → candidate benchmark → promotion gate.

The held-out set is used only as a final regression guardrail. It must not be used to generate proposals or tune the candidate.

  a Claude Code session. Detected about 1.5 min after deploy, rolled back automatically, verified by
  replays Scout ran itself (3/3), resolved in under 3 min. The postmortem quotes the coding agent's

```

| Path | What |
|---|---|
| `backend/nightshift/` | Detector, investigator, provenance (git + Entire + entire-graph), impact, policy, actions, verifier, reporter, adapters, neatlogs sources |
| `backend/product/` | Workspaces, agents, encrypted secrets, Slack app, paging, GitHub fix PRs, repo clones |
| `backend/api/` | FastAPI: product API, SDK endpoints, Slack endpoints, sandbox, SSE |
| `sdk/python/` | `nightshift-sdk` |
| `backend/harbor/` | Harbor, the refunds support agent (releases r42–r46 written by coding-agent sessions) |
